title: 0/1 Knapsack: The Shape Behind Subset-Sum Problems
oneLiner: Pick a subset of items, each usable at most once, to maximize value within a weight limit -- one descending loop is the entire difference from letting an item be reused.
keyTakeaway: The inner loop over capacity w MUST run DESCENDING (from the limit down to the item's weight) -- that single direction is what keeps every item usable at most once. Running it ascending would let dp[w] see this SAME item's own update earlier in the same pass, silently turning 0/1 knapsack (each item once) into unbounded knapsack (each item any number of times).
explanation:
Given a set of items, each with a weight and a value, and a capacity limit, choose a SUBSET of items (each used at most once -- that's the "0/1": take it or don't) to maximize total value without exceeding the weight capacity. This is the shape underneath a whole family of problems that don't look like it at first -- "can this array be partitioned into two equal-sum halves," "does some subset sum to exactly X" -- all of them are 0/1 knapsack with the value function simplified away.

The space-optimized solution keeps a single 1D array dp[w] = the best value achievable with total weight AT MOST w, all zeros to start (for "exactly w" you'd set dp[0] = 0 and every other entry to minus infinity, so unreachable weights can't win). Process items ONE AT A TIME; for each item (weight wt, value v), loop w from the full capacity DOWN TO wt, updating dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w-wt] + v) -- "either skip this item (keep dp[w] as-is) or take it (dp[w-wt] plus this item's value)." The descending direction is the entire trick: it guarantees dp[w-wt] on the right-hand side still reflects the PREVIOUS item's state, not this item's own just-written update -- reading ascending would let this exact item get folded into its own answer more than once.

Watch the dp array evolve below, one item at a time -- by the end, dp[capacity] holds the best achievable value using any subset of the items shown.

starterCode.python:
def knapsack(weights, values, capacity):
    # TODO: dp[w] = best value achievable with capacity w, all zeros
    # to start. For each item (weight wt, value v): for w from
    # capacity DOWN TO wt: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - wt] + v). The
    # DESCENDING inner loop is what keeps each item usable at most
    # once. Return dp[capacity].
    return 0

recognitionSignals: You're choosing a SUBSET of items, each usable at most once, to maximize (or minimize) some value subject to a capacity/budget/weight limit.
The problem is a variant of "can a subset sum to exactly X" or "partition into two equal groups" -- these are 0/1 knapsack wearing different clothes.
gotchas: The inner loop over w MUST run DESCENDING (capacity down to the item's weight) -- ascending lets the same item get added to dp[w] more than once, turning 0/1 knapsack into unbounded knapsack by accident.
dp[w - wt] on the right-hand side needs to still be the PREVIOUS item's value at that index -- that's only guaranteed by the descending order, not an accident of the formula itself.
confusableWith: Dynamic Programming: Climbing Stairs (Fundamentals track) fills a 1D dp array too, but every cell only ever depends on EARLIER cells filled in the same left-to-right pass -- knapsack's descending inner loop exists specifically to avoid that kind of same-item reuse within one item's pass.

complexity.note: n items times W capacities, each cell O(1); the 1-D rolling array needs only W+1 cells (the 2-D version needs n·W).
